title: 道德消费需要易于识别、可及且负担得起，尤其是在经济恶化的情况下。而且我们需要重新思考我们应该为经济优化什么—— LessWrong
author: Portia
content:
I don’t know anyone who wants the rainforest, which is storing carbon and biodiversity and undiscovered medicines for us all, to be burned down for their coffee, and the people harvesting it paid too little to live a dignified life.

I don’t know anyone who wants the animals they eat to be mutilated without anaesthesia, to be trapped in overcrowded conditions without ever seeing the sun, to not receive medical care, to be slowly gassed to death.

I don’t know anyone who wants their clothing to be made by children working long days under dangerous conditions instead of going to school.

I don’t know anyone who wants our soil and water to become unbalanced or poisonous to our native animals through rampant overuse of artificial fertiliser and pesticides.


And yet the vast majority of products bought in the West contribute to exactly this. This isn’t because the consumers are bad people who want to make the world a worse place by being in it. This is the world we ourselves live in, that our friends and children will live in, why would we want it to sicken? Why would we want other people, and innocent animals, to be tortured for no good reason? 

People buy what they do because they want to feed and clothe their families, survive each day, and because they are simply tired. Inflation is eating our savings, if we have any; many of us haven’t just stopped saving, but are slipping into debt. The costs for food, rent, heating, mobility are skyrocketing. Yet our wages are not rising. Promotions are being postponed, empty positions not replaced, with us expected to work more without more pay, and more and more of us burning out. Degrees or a can do attitude no longer guarantee work. Many of us are finding our jobs being replaced by AI, leaving people without jobs they did well and liked doing and that paid them a living wage, while AI does the job less transparently, less reliably, with less of a human touch, and while there are thus fewer and fewer jobs – how is this compatible with the general good? It means some people will systematically end up out of work, but there is no universal basic income forthcoming, the welfare that is given is tied to shame, and itself increasingly cut and lowered when it is already not matching the rising costs of living. At my age, my parents were buying a house. My peers and I are struggling to find anything we can afford to rent and keep at a bearable temperature.


And the vicious circle of it all is part of the worst of it. People can’t upgrade to newer appliances or switch to green contracts, so they waste electricity made by burning coal. They can’t renovate their homes, so they waste fuel to heat them which releases even more CO2 into the atmosphere, and then bake in the Summers that climate change makes ever worse. Trains are ever more expensive and unreliable, e-cars are unaffordable, and so people continue driving their petrol cars that poison the air. People can’t afford to buy fairtrade products, and realise their poverty is reproduced on a scale incomprehensibly worse across the planet. They can’t afford organic food, and know insect populations are collapsing around us. They are constantly stressed and tired while navigating a landscape in which you often need to do research just to figure out which is the most ethical option, if any of this packaging material can actually be recycled, whether the animal welfare claim means anything at all. It is grossly inefficient for each individual. And it will make things harder for all of us in the long run.


I’m not disputing that ethical choices are still possible in this world. We do have options left, and something is better that nothing.

What I am pointing out is that the behaviour we would want everyone to show to heal our planet and injustice, the behaviour that the vast majority of us actually want to show, is made systematically difficult, and thus de facto fails to reliably materialise for the vast majority of people, and guilting them and pointing out the remaining possibilities has not substantially changed that.

In our societies - the richest in the world! - behaving ethically in our consumer choices is increasingly, and with justification, seen as something only the most privileged can think about. That is crazy.


The solution to that is not more guilt. Guilt is seldomly a productive emotion.


Instead, here are some ideas for proposals for our governments, for us to lobby for.


  1. Specifically, and exclusively, direct subsidies towards ethical products; in particular, do not subsidise unethical products. Do not subsidise or bail out petrol, flights, industrialised meat production, overuse of pesticides or financial speculation. Do subsidise a switch to renewables, reliable and safe public transportation, farming practices that keep our land healthy, produce plant based proteins, and treat animals with kindness and respect. Pouring tax money into products that make the world worse is incomprehensible.
  2. Introduce mandatory, clearly defined and non-ambiguous, verified labelling for degrees of ethical practices behind goods. A consumer should see at a glance whether the chickens laying these eggs could roam outside. This labelling should continue beyond the original product. E.g. there is currently zero incentive for any restaurant to purchase ethical produce, because the origin and composition of their products is not displayed in any way. Yes, this is work. But it is far less work to do it for products and them have every consumer see it at a glance, than for each consumer to try to figure this out with nothing but a smartphone while in a rush in the supermarket.
  3. Outlaw practices that fall below what we consider ethically acceptable, enable ways to not break these laws in practice, and verify that these laws are not broken. Outlaw them specifically both inside our own countries, and outlaw the imports of products produced under such conditions abroad to prevent displacement. E.g. having outlawed battery farms for eggs in Europe, we shouldn’t important cakes made with eggs from battery farms, and sell them to our local consumers who have no idea. 
  4. You cannot simultaneously «optimise» our economy by stripping human labour for it and blocking people from the labour market, and then make providing human labour a precondition to a dignified life. We have humans who need resources, and who are willing and able to work to provide them. Make this easy. E.g. make it possible, with low bureaucratic hurdles, to start up businesses, or provide independent services for each other. It should be easy to offer babysitting, cleaning, repairs, construction, moving help or chauffeuring services, or to sell things you grow or create, to bring forth a new product that people actually need - you shouldn't need a work contract with a huge number of preconditions and consequences to do something productive and be paid for it. Do not punish people for re-entering the labour market.
  5. Where there is work that needs to be done, and humans who like doing it and have no better alternative, it isn’t optimisation to strip humans from it by adding resource sucking tech and stress. Like, we do need more public green, greened roofs and facades, solar mounted everywhere. Humans like creating art, writing texts, teaching, gardening, it is good for us to do. I would rather have a bunch of people calmly and quietly take their time to look after the greenery in my area, planting trees, watering plants, just clipping and raking by hand where it is necessary, and be paid for this – instead of being given welfare by an agency that judges them for burning out in modern workplaces, and having them sit at home feeling useless, and just have one person go through with loud, oil sucking machinery and butcher everything green while stressing the entire neighbourhood with the noise. I think everyone involved – the people working, the people living in the area – would prefer this. So why are we optimising for something else?
  6. If we seriously do not need remotely as much work to be done as there are people who need to do work to be paid a living wage, and we'd just be occupying people to keep them busy – then don't punish people for accordingly not working, or force them to do mindless things that no-one needs, but set them free in a dignified manner. Instead, consider universal basic income, and empowering and valuing other work they do in looking after children, the elderly, looking after their neighbourhoods, doing activism and being creative. I'd rather have the cashier down the street look after her kids and paint public murals than work behind a cash desk that has her bored out of her mind, just because she knows that if she didn't have this pointless job that can in fact be replaced cheaply by a machine, she would lose all public respect and security. Her human dignity should be independent of that. Her contribution to society is not logically reflected in this wage.


Very happy to hear other and better suggestions, or issues with the ones I have raised. Economics isn’t my field; I am just looking at what is going on around me and thinking, whatever this is, it isn’t fit for purpose.


The whole point of our economy, of money itself and our subsidies in particular, of our laws and our bureaucracy, should be to enable better lives. It is why they were invented. We made them up; we can change them if they are not fit for purpose as is. They are not goals in and off themselves, they are tools to help everyone, and should be aligned with our values.

If people are on average less happy, and acting less ethically, feel all their choices are bad and make them feel like they are not themselves, not doing as much good as they can, not getting the respect they need; if non-humans animals are less happy, if our very planet and climate is getting sick in a way that endangers us all; then I don’t care what the numbers say, we are setting our priorities and incentives wrong and need to rethink them.
aiSummary: 文章认为，道德消费在成本、可及性和内疚感方面系统受阻，并提出六项政策行动——对道德商品提供补贴、明确标签、禁止不道德行为、支持人力劳动、抵制不必要的自动化以及考虑全民基本收入——以使经济激励与社会福祉保持一致。
oneSentenceSummary: 文章认为，道德消费在成本、可及性和内疚感方面系统受阻，并提出六项政策行动——对道德商品提供补贴、明确标签、禁止不道德行为、支持人力劳动、抵制不必要的自动化以及考虑全民基本收入——以使经济激励与社会福祉保持一致。
summary: 作者一开始指出，几乎没有人希望环境破坏、动物虐待、剥削性劳动或生态危害，但大多数西方购买却导致这些结果。他解释说，消费者在能够的时候会采取道德行为，但结构性压力——工资停滞、生活成本上升、就业不安全以及验证道德主张所需的耗时努力——使得负责任的选择变得困难，形成一个削弱个人福祉和地球健康的恶性循环。虽然承认道德选择仍然存在，作者认为内疚感无效，而是为政府提供具体的政策建议，专门补贴道德产品，强制要求易于阅读且经过验证的道德标签，且标签应超出产品本身，禁止被视为不道德的行为（包括在这些条件下生产的进口商品），降低小规模人力劳动服务的官僚障碍，反对用不必要的自动化取代有意义的人力工作，并在工作稀缺时提供有尊严的全民基本收入，同时重视照料、创造和社区工作。文章最后指出，经济、货币、补贴、法律和官僚体系应作为工具来实现更好的生活，而非目的本身，必须重新与人类和生态价值观保持一致。

mainPoints.point: 道德消费受到成本、可及性以及验证主张所需努力的阻碍。
mainPoints.explanation: 尽管人们反对环境破坏、动物虐待和不公平劳动，但工资停滞、通胀以及识别真正道德产品所需的耗时研究使得大多数人负责任的选择变得系统性困难。

mainPoints.point: 内疚感是推动系统性变革的无效动机。
mainPoints.explanation: 作者认为内疚感很少能产生积极行动，因此不应依赖它来驱动道德行为。

mainPoints.point: 政府应仅对道德产品和实践提供补贴。
mainPoints.explanation: 直接财政支持应指向可再生能源、安全公共交通、再生农业、植物蛋白和人道动物待遇，而对化石燃料、工业肉类、过量农药和金融投机的补贴应被取消。

mainPoints.point: 应强制要求商品使用清晰、明确且经过验证的道德标签，且标签应超出产品本身。
mainPoints.explanation: 标签将使消费者能够立即看到，例如鸡蛋是否来自散养鸡，并且还会激励餐厅和零售商采购道德产品，因为这些信息将在销售点可见。

mainPoints.point: 不道德行为应在国内和进口中被禁止，并提供合规支持。
mainPoints.explanation: 例如，禁止笼养鸡场必须伴随防止在这些条件下生产的商品进口的措施，以确保法律不会通过转移被规避。

mainPoints.point: 经济政策应促进人力劳动、抵制不必要的自动化，并考虑全民基本收入。
mainPoints.explanation: 降低小型服务的官僚障碍、重视人们享受的工作（照料、创造和社区），并在工作稀缺时提供有尊严的基本收入，将使经济激励与人类福祉保持一致，而不仅仅是优化劳动削减。

keyQuotes: 解决办法不是更多的内疚。
我们有人需要资源，并且愿意且能够工作来提供这些资源。让这变得容易。
我们的经济、货币本身以及特别是我们的补贴、法律和官僚体系的全部目的，应该是使人们过上更好的生活。
